/society/2026/oct/09/nhs-fonagy-review-a.headline: No ‘snowflakes’: mental health review says today’s youth have it harder and harms are real
/society/2026/oct/09/nhs-fonagy-review-a.excerpt: Eighteen months ago, in an off-the-cuff remark during a discussion on disability benefit cuts, Wes Streeting said mental health conditions were being “overdiagnosed”, riding headlong into another culture war. He later apologised for the comment, but at the time it seemed the then health secretary had endorsed a populist view that ordinary stresses and disappointments had become too often medicalised, resulting in a surge of bogus clinical diagnoses and creating a “snowflake generation” of fragile, avoidant and workshy young people. Prof Peter Fonagy’s mammoth review of mental health conditions, autism and ADHD in England, commissioned by Streeting nine months ago, has no truck with the snowflake generation caricature: the steep rise in the prevalence of mental health problems such as anxiety and depression is real, he says, and so is the distress and difficulties they can cause. I am in awe of their courage. Young people are contending with more powerful forces than I ever faced The review says the drivers of this rise are cultural and social. Young people are exposed to Covid disruption, financial and housing insecurity, and competitive school and social stresses that are exacerbated by social media. Support services, from Sure Start to youth clubs, have been swept away. There is less belonging, it says, and more loneliness. Fonagy himself was a severely depressed teenager in 1960s London, he reveals in an unexpectedly tender foreword to the review.
/society/2026/oct/09/nhs-fonagy-review-a.trail: Peter Fonagy lauds courage of young people and warns of consequences of rising prevalence of mental illness

/society/2026/oct/09/nhs-fonagy-review-a.headline: NHS England mental health services review: what has it found and what does it recommend?
/society/2026/oct/09/nhs-fonagy-review-a.excerpt: The Fonagy review of NHS England’s mental health, ADHD and autism services was commissioned in 2025 by Wes Streeting, then the health secretary, in response to growing concerns that spiralling waiting lists for assessment, diagnosis and care threatened the NHS’s ability to meet the demand. The 607-page report, published on Friday, says that without a radical overhaul, mental health and neurodiversity services will be overwhelmed. Here are some of its key findings and recommendations. Unprecedented and growing levels of distress are real The report is categoric that mental distress has “increased substantially across the population”, is real and affects everyday functioning, and that the rise “cannot be explained by greater awareness alone”. About one in four 16- to 24-year-olds are now thought to have a common mental disorder such as anxiety and depression, up from one in six in 1993, while self-harm, eating disorders, OCD, PTSD and drug dependence have also increased. About 4 million children are in “serious distress”, and if current trends continue that could reach 4.5 million by 2030, the report says. At current rates self-harm cases could reach 2.5 million across England’s population. But rates of severe mental illness such as bipolar or schizophrenia have remained much more stable, while hazardous drinking has declined.
/society/2026/oct/09/nhs-fonagy-review-a.trail: Prof Peter Fonagy’s 607-page report is categoric that mental distress has increased substantially and ‘cannot be explained by greater awareness alone’

/society/2026/oct/09/nhs-fonagy-review-a.headline: ‘Early deaths are not inevitable’: report reveals why adults with severe mental illness die younger
/society/2026/oct/09/nhs-fonagy-review-a.excerpt: An analysis of NHS data has shed light on the “scandal” of why adults with severe mental illness are more likely to die 15 to 20 years younger than the general population. The Rethink Mental Illness charity has revealed that adults under 75 with serious mental ill health – defined as those referred to specialist secondary mental health services – are 6.3 times as likely to die from liver disease, 6 times more likely from respiratory illness, 3.8 times more likely from cardiovascular disease and 2.3 times as likely from cancer. They are also 14.6 times as likely to die due to suicide, compared with those who were not referred. Overall, they are 4.8 times more likely to die of any cause before the age of 75 than the general population. For some conditions, these health inequalities are the starkest to date. For working-age adults living with a mental illness, the number of deaths from cardiovascular disease and cancer are at their highest levels since records began, each with more than 24,000 deaths in the 2022-2024 reporting period, the charity calculated. Cancer, cardiovascular disease, liver disease and respiratory disease accounted for more than half (56.5%) of deaths for 18- to 74-year-olds with severe mental health problems in England during this period. Cancer and cardiovascular disease each accounted for just under 19% of all deaths, respiratory disease 11%, and liver disease 8%. During the same period, suicide comprised 7% of these early deaths.
/society/2026/oct/09/nhs-fonagy-review-a.trail: Exclusive: Charity says NHS data shows increased chances of death due to preventable physical illnesses

/society/2026/oct/09/nhs-fonagy-review-a.headline: Plan to limit NHS diagnoses of ADHD attacked as ‘rationing’ healthcare
/society/2026/oct/09/nhs-fonagy-review-a.excerpt: Proposals to limit the number of patients being formally diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder have been attacked as “rationing” healthcare and pushing children and adults to self-diagnosis via social media. The comments came before a government review due next week, which is expected to say that patients with ADHD symptoms should not automatically be formally diagnosed, but should be “triaged” and offered support without the need for a formal diagnosis. Details of this “needs-based” system, first revealed in the Times, would mean NHS services target those most acutely affected by ADHD, such as those at risk of self-harm or unable to work. Less severely affected people may not be referred for a formal diagnosis to NHS clinics but would be offered help according to a “holistic” assessment of their needs, the report will say. The government’s independent review of mental health conditions, autism and ADHD was commissioned in December by the then health secretary, Wes Streeting, amid concerns over the sharp rise of people making sickness benefit claims due to mental health, autism and ADHD diagnoses. Led by Prof Peter Fonagy, a clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst at University College London, the interim review concluded that the system forces children and adults to obtain a formal diagnosis in order to get support. Official figures show that patients are waiting years to be assessed, with 800,000 on NHS waiting lists.
/society/2026/oct/09/nhs-fonagy-review-a.trail: Review expected to say patients in England should be ‘triaged’ and offered support without formal diagnosis

/society/2026/oct/09/nhs-fonagy-review-a.headline: ‘A really scary place for children’: English hospitals have chronic lack of health play staff
/society/2026/oct/09/nhs-fonagy-review-a.excerpt: Children in English hospitals with serious illnesses are being exposed to avoidable trauma because too few health play professionals are being employed, analysis by a leading charity has found. These workers help to support children through the trauma and anxiety that can come with receiving medical treatment while in hospital by providing play opportunities through games, toys and activities. However, the hospitals are facing a shortage of such staff, leaving children without the relief such organised play and games can provide for those having treatment for serious conditions. Across NHS hospitals, there are only 955 full-time equivalent health play professionals currently supporting 21 million child hospital admissions each year, according to figures obtained by the charity Starlight Children’s Foundation via freedom of information requests. This equates to a ratio of about one professional for every 22,061 admissions, far below the recommended staffing levels of one professional per 2,230 hospital admissions. In England, there are 820 health play professionals supporting almost 17m admissions. Health play professionals can also help to provide positive healthcare experiences for children, which research has shown can help to reduce distress, improve cooperation and help to prevent lifelong healthcare avoidance and mental health problems associated with traumatic childhood healthcare experiences.
/society/2026/oct/09/nhs-fonagy-review-a.trail: Analysis finds only 955 play professionals supporting 21 million child hospital admissions, leaving many traumatised for life

/uk-news/2026/oct/08/last-hours-three-si.headline: Cities in Great Britain most vulnerable to extreme heat revealed
/uk-news/2026/oct/08/last-hours-three-si.excerpt: Portsmouth, Leicester, Exeter, Bristol and Nottingham will be among the cities that warm the most by the end of this century as global heating turns British cities into urban heat islands, according to research. Analysis from Ordnance Survey (OS) has created a heat vulnerability index for all cities in Great Britain. Portsmouth, which sits on the south coast of England and is home to 208,000 people, is the most vulnerable to extreme heat today and into the future, according to the research from the OS, the Met Office and the data analysis company 4 Earth Intelligence. Concrete, asphalt, buildings and hard surfaces in cities absorb solar radiation during the day and act like giant radiators, holding on to the heat rather than cooling down at night as in more rural areas. Cities can be up to 10C hotter than surrounding areas. Areas most at risk of extreme warming are those with the least tree cover, green space and waterways. This summer was provisionally the UK’s hottest on record, and the research reveals which cities are suffering now from intense urban heat and which will be among the warmest in future. The research analyses 71 cities granted by royal charter across England, Scotland and Wales but excluding Northern Ireland. The OS heat vulnerability index suggests that by 2040 all 71 cities will reach high heat vulnerability. By the turn of the century, almost two-thirds could reach the most severe level.
/uk-news/2026/oct/08/last-hours-three-si.trail: OS index examines which ‘urban heat islands’ suffer the most – and which cope the best with rising temperatures

/world/2026/oct/08/france-student-protes.headline: Thursday briefing: Why young people are taking to the streets across France
/world/2026/oct/08/france-student-protes.excerpt: Good morning. In my experience, at any protest, the most memorable and encapsulating slogans are always the ones written by hand with marker pen on cardboard placards. “School is a right, not a privilege,” read one such sign held aloft by a student in Paris, where huge youth protests over the state of high school education have brought tens of thousands of young people and adults on to the streets, with further strikes planned today. “A state that gasses high school students is a weak state,” another sign said, referencing growing public anger at alleged police brutality towards young protesters. Tens of thousands of young people have also taken to Spanish streets in recent weeks to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis. And outside the Labour conference in Liverpool last week, a crowd of jobless young people protested against what they saw as their bleak employment prospects. From Paris to the north of England, a similar thread runs through it all: a generation who feel betrayed by the absence of basic economic security and the erosion of public services that older generations took for granted. I spoke to our Paris correspondent Angelique Chrisafis who has been reporting from the centre of the French protests. But first, the headlines. Five big stories UK politics | Kemi Badenoch has announced that the Conservatives would abolish inheritance tax on family homes if elected, prompting criticism that she is prioritising cutting taxes for the rich.

/world/2026/oct/08/france-student-protes.headline: French police suspend use of stun grenades at school protests as minister rejects accusations of brutality
/world/2026/oct/08/france-student-protes.excerpt: France’s interior minister has suspended the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations but rejected mounting accusations of police brutality during two weeks of protests marred by often violent clashes that have injured hundreds. Laurent Nuñez told RTL radio on Wednesday that he had ordered a temporary halt on the use of the grenades “in the context of the high school students’ movement” after a 15-year-old boy lost a hand during a protest in Lens, northern France, on Monday. Authorities have not confirmed the exact circumstances – in particular, whether the boy had picked up the grenade or been struck by it – but said up to 200 protesters had been hurling projectiles at police when the riot squad intervened. Nuñez said he was suspending use of the grenades “until we know exactly what happened in this case”. But he later told MPs that accusations of “police repression” were “excessive” because officers “are not intervening if the protests are peaceful”. The injured boy’s mother said on Wednesday that her son’s hand had been amputated. She told BFMTV: “His life has been stolen. He’s a 15-year-old kid, how can children be treated like that?” She said her son had not tried to pick up the grenade. The education ministry said classes had been wholly or partially suspended in 429 of the country’s 3,700 lycées – high schools attended by pupils aged between 15 and 18 – on Wednesday, a significantly lower number than on Tuesday.
/world/2026/oct/08/france-student-protes.trail: Minister says use of grenades has been stopped after a student lost a hand as protests across France continue

/world/2026/oct/08/france-student-protes.headline: Riot police fire teargas as 250,000 take part in schools protests across France
/world/2026/oct/08/france-student-protes.excerpt: Police have fired teargas at ⁠protesters as more than 250,000 pupils, teachers and parents demonstrated across France on the biggest day yet of a campaign for better high school conditions that has been marred by often violent clashes with police. The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said at least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff had been injured since the protests began more than a fortnight ago, calling the figures “the heaviest ⁠toll in decades paid by the school system”. The country’s president, Emmanuel Macron, called key ministers to the Élysée Palace for talks on Tuesday night, French media reported. The interior ministry said 200,000 people had taken part in mainly peaceful marches in cities including Marseille, Nantes ⁠and Lyon on Tuesday, with 56,000 more joining the biggest demonstration in Paris. Organisers put the total at 450,000. Most passed off without serious incident, but some – including in Paris – ended in sporadic vandalism and running skirmishes with riot police, with officers firing teargas and carrying out baton charges to disperse protesters. Nearly 500 people were arrested on Tuesday, according to figures from the Interior Ministry reported by newspaper Liberation. The ministry also said 43 police officers were injured.

/world/2026/oct/08/france-student-protes.headline: ‘This is state violence’: Paris students rage at politicians and heavy-handed policing
/world/2026/oct/08/france-student-protes.excerpt: Before dawn on Tuesday outside the Lycée Sophie-Germain in central Paris, hundreds of teenagers dragged wheelie bins, metal barriers and shopping trolleys to build a barricade outside the front door of their secondary school. Climbing to the top of the piles of bins, pupils held banners calling for more funding and greater equality in French schools. But they were also protesting against French riot police, who have been accused by human rights groups of using disproportionate force against children in what is fast becoming the biggest youth protest movement in decades. “Everyone hates the police,” chanted a group of 15- and 16-year-olds. At least 215 teenagers, 715 police officers and 85 teaching staff have been injured in clashes in recent days, according to the government. “We’re teenagers with wheelie bins, and the police have heavy weapons, it’s totally mismatched,” said Livia, 17, who was studying theatre at a lycée in northern Paris and did not want her real name published. “The police are extremely violent in France. This is state violence and it’s horrible seeing police allowed to target children.
/world/2026/oct/08/france-student-protes.trail: Unprecedented protests that began in low-income suburb are turning ugly, with investigations under way into police brutality

/world/2026/oct/08/france-student-protes.headline: France braces for national day of school protests as boy loses hand
/world/2026/oct/08/france-student-protes.excerpt: France is bracing for a national day of protests and high-school blockades as a youth protest movement gathers pace amid a growing debate over the scale of the police response. In one incident, a 15-year-old protesting against what demonstrators said were France’s dilapidated ⁠and understaffed schools ‌had his hand ‌blown off outside a high school in the northern town of Lens, said François-Xavier Lauch, the prefect of Pas-de-Calais. Lauch declined to comment on the exact circumstances, but said between 150 and 200 protesters had been hurling a series of objects at police when riot officers intervened. It was uncertain if the incident had involved a police stun grenade or how the injury happened. Lauch said an investigation had been opened. The family of a 16-year-old school pupil in Tours also filed a complaint about police violence after he lost sight in his right eye last week. The state prosecutor said the boy’s injuries were in line with the impact from a police rubber bullet. A police investigation is under way. The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, had earlier attempted to calm the protests by accepting schoolchildren’s grievances as “legitimate” and saying the government must listen. Lecornu ordered ministers to tackle the students’ five major demands. These include organising the replacement of absent teachers, in recognition that pupils in some areas miss months of teaching because of staff absences – even in key exam years.

/world/2026/oct/09/japan-royal-throne-li.headline: Extreme heat warnings issued for parts of southern California
/world/2026/oct/09/japan-royal-throne-li.excerpt: The National Weather Service in the US has issued extreme heat warnings for parts of southern California, including Los Angeles, until Thursday, as temperatures are expected to hit the high 30s celsius. Burbank, a suburb north of Los Angeles, recorded 39C on Saturday, a few degrees shy of the October record for the region set in 1987. A persistent area of high pressure will remain in place this week, leading to further hazardous hot weather and increased fire risk. Parts of Indonesia are in the midst of an extreme wildfire season, which has peaked over the past month. Western Kalimantan (Borneo) and southern Sumatra have been particularly badly affected. The lack of rainfall has dried the usually water-logged tropical soils, meaning that fires have been able to spread quickly, above and below the surface. Indonesia’s soils are also extremely rich in peat, meaning that the smoke produced from the fires contain higher levels of toxic gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide. Cities in surrounding areas and as far as Malaysia and Singapore have experienced reduced air quality in recent weeks as a result. Drought and wildfires are more common in this part of the world during El Niño events owing to suppressed thunderstorm activity. On the flip side, El Niño is contributing to an extremely active period for tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean.

/world/2026/oct/09/japan-royal-throne-li.headline: AI tool that copied actor’s ‘lustrous’ voice violated his rights, Tokyo court rules
/world/2026/oct/09/japan-royal-throne-li.excerpt: A court in Japan has ruled that the human voice has legal protection after a landmark case involving a well-known actor and a TikTok account that he claimed had cloned his “lustrous” baritone voice in its AI-generated videos. Tokyo district court said on Wednesday that voices should enjoy the same protection as publicity rights, at the end of a closely watched legal action brought against TikTok by Kenjiro Tsuda – best known for voicing the character Kento Nanami in the anime Jujutsu Kaisen. But the court dismissed Tsuda’s request that the operator of TikTok remove the videos, noting that the user had deleted them soon after the suit was filed last November. “The unauthorised use of a performer’s voice … can be considered an infringement on publicity rights,” said the presiding judge, Aya Takahashi. The lawsuit is believed to be the first in Japan seeking to defend an individual’s vocal identity against AI-generated copies. Japan’s voice actors, many of whom achieve star status through their “appearances” in anime, are increasingly worried that AI mimicry is threatening their livelihoods and the industry as a whole. An actor’s voice “is the result of years of rigorous training and apprenticeship”, Yuko Sasaki, executive director of the Japan Actors Union said ahead of the ruling. Tsuda, 55, claimed that the 188 TikTok videos uploaded on an anonymous account between July 2024 and September last year had been narrated by a “deep” and “lustrous” voice that could only be his.
/world/2026/oct/09/japan-royal-throne-li.trail: Kenjiro Tsuda secures partial victory against TikTok account in landmark Japanese verdict to protect publicity rights

/world/2026/oct/09/japan-royal-throne-li.headline: As Japan swelters, farmers turn to new heat-resistant rice varieties to boost staple crop
/world/2026/oct/09/japan-royal-throne-li.excerpt: When schoolchildren in Shiroishi were enlisted to plant rice seedlings in June, Shinto priests blessed the land and asked the deities for a bountiful crop. Judging by the fields behind farmer Haruki Kawasaki, their prayers have been answered. The 63-year-old is preparing to harvest this year’s crop of hinatamaru, a variety of rice whose plump grains have thrived despite exposure to another hot and dry summer, conditions that typically punish rice yields. Hinatamaru is one of growing number of heat-resistant rice varieties that are giving fresh hope to farmers across Japan that they can overcome a climate emergency that is threatening the country’s staple crop. Kawasaki and his team once spent the entire day in the fields, but the heat has made that impossible. “Now we start early in the morning and work until around noon,” he says. “It’s way too hot in the afternoon … although the mornings are not what you would call cool.” Kawasaki and other farmers in Saga are at the centre of the boom as Japan finds ways to cope with a warmer future. The long process of developing heat-tolerant strains involves cross-breeding existing varieties, cultivation in controlled environments and, finally, real-world trials. Japan’s ageing farmers have toiled through record-breaking heat and below-average rainfall over the last three summers. After heat records were broken again this year, the meteorological agency added a new category – “cruelly hot days” – when the mercury exceeds 40C.
/world/2026/oct/09/japan-royal-throne-li.trail: New rice varieties give hope that farmers can overcome the climate emergency and a warmer future that threatens harvests

/world/2026/oct/09/japan-royal-throne-li.headline: Japanese islands brace for Dujuan to become a typhoon again
/world/2026/oct/09/japan-royal-throne-li.excerpt: Tropical Storm Dujuan is skirting the coast of Japan and despite avoiding a direct landfall, is still expected to leave its mark. Dujuan briefly reached typhoon status on Friday before weakening to a tropical storm again on Sunday morning. But it is expected to restrengthen back to a typhoon by Tuesday morning. Sustained winds could reach 80mph (129km/h), with gusts approaching 100mph. Although mainland Japan has avoided a direct hit, Dujuan’s track takes it across the Izu Islands, where evacuation warnings are in place. Heavy rain, flooding and landslide alerts are widespread, with high waves adding another threat to exposed coastal areas and islands. Some exceptional rainfall totals are expected, with about 200mm (7.9in) possible along the southern coasts of the Chubu and Kanto regions in just 24 hours – roughly equivalent to the average rainfall for the entire month of September. The Tokyo metropolitan area is among the areas facing the heaviest rain, with some models suggesting nearly 90mm could fall within six hours on Monday evening. Further south, the Izu peninsula could receive more than 80mm in just three hours – 38% of the month’s usual rainfall in a single evening. Dujuan is expected to continue north-eastwards before dissipating in the north-west Pacific later this week. The Atlantic hurricane season remains unusually quiet, despite Tropical Storm Fay developing south-west of the Azores over the weekend.
/world/2026/oct/09/japan-royal-throne-li.trail: Storm system expected to hit Izu Islands as it strengthens. Meanwhile, Atlantic hurricane season is unusually quiet

/world/2026/oct/09/japan-royal-throne-li.headline: Weather tracker: Thunderstorms hit Spain as Japan braces for typhoon
/world/2026/oct/09/japan-royal-throne-li.excerpt: Intense and slow-moving thunderstorms broke out on Wednesday afternoon across parts of eastern Spain, bringing some severe flooding and killing at least one person. Storms first struck over the Castilla-La Mancha region during the afternoon before passing over Spain’s east coast, becoming very slow-moving and continuing overnight. Torrential rainfall, strong winds and large hail were reported in Valencia and Barcelona, causing widespread flooding in both cities. Weather stations west of Barcelona recorded some of the highest totals with more than 100mm (4in) of rain falling in the space of a few hours, and locally 70mm in just 30 minutes in the early hours of Thursday morning. Cars and roads were submerged, and flights were cancelled across the region. Wednesday’s La Liga fixture between Levante and Athletic Club had to be postponed due to flooding at the Estadio Ciudad de Valencia. On Thursday rescuers found the body of a man near Olivella, west of Barcelona, after his car was swept away in the waters. Spain’s east coast is susceptible to extreme rainfall during the autumn months, as experienced in 2024, when devastating flash floods killed more than 200 people in Valencia. With the Mediterranean Sea reaching record temperatures, this is providing extra fuel and moisture to thunderstorms, making flooding more likely. In New Jersey in the US on Sunday, the Racefaster half marathon was disrupted due to extreme rainfall and a partly submerged course.

/environment/2026/oct/09/plant-selfie-ja.headline: Country diary: An autumn bounty of fruits is well on its way
/environment/2026/oct/09/plant-selfie-ja.excerpt: It is rare for me to visit the same place twice within a couple of weeks, but my walk in the Teifi Marshes recently was curtailed by heavy rain, and I feel that I have unfinished business. Last time I started from the Cilgerran end of the marsh, so today begin at the seaward side – crossing the bridge over the Teifi and heading upstream past the site of the old, sadly long-departed Cardigan railway station. My route follows the former course of the railway line, but I briefly divert along a boardwalk into the broad reedbeds at the heart of the marsh. Here, I am surrounded by the ambient sound of the wind in the reeds, which ebbs and flows with an almost animate organic static – pushing back the distant sounds of traffic on the main road. Scrub and small trees interact with the reeds at the margins, their autumn bounty of fruits already well advanced. The blackberries are almost over, but the sloes are plump and mature with the promise of a warming winter spirit to come. Back on the main trail, a weasel, a low blur of fur and legs, dashes across the path in front of me just as the sun emerges from banks of grey cloud. The new shadows make me look up. Beyond the mile or so of reedbed, the valley side is wooded with deciduous trees just beginning to fade into autumn colours. Among them, a few bare crowns of what I take to be dead ash trees stand skeletal, awaiting the winter storm. The Afon Teifi is tidal here, and it is about an hour after high water.
/environment/2026/oct/09/plant-selfie-ja.trail: Cardigan: Taking a walk beside the River Teifi, I encounter trees beginning to fade into new season colour, and the low blur of a weasel

/environment/2026/oct/09/plant-selfie-ja.headline: Country diary: A lesson from my final diary after nearly 40 years – keep looking closely
/environment/2026/oct/09/plant-selfie-ja.excerpt: After another exceptionally dry summer, there’s a nagging question lurking at the back of naturalists’ minds: which species will be the winners and losers in our evolving climate? Throughout summer’s heatwaves and drought, I watched a dense stand of broad-leaved docks, Rumex obtusifolius, thrive while surrounding fields turned the colour of bleached straw. They have promising credentials as drought survivors, thanks to a deep taproot, fast, early spring growth and a long-lasting dormant seed bank in the soil. “One year’s seeding, seven years weeding” goes the old adage, warning of the consequences of allowing weed seeds to ripen and disperse on cultivated ground. That’s an over-optimistic outlook in the case of docks, whose buried seeds can remain viable for up to 80 years. They need light to germinate, but some of today’s bumper seed crop, brought to the surface by burrowing animals eight decades hence, could conceivably grow, flower and set seeds in the early years of the 22nd century. Broad-leaved dock, growing as a weed, has colonised cultivated land since the earliest days of British agriculture. As a wildflower, it’s a rather coarse, unattractive but medicinally useful ruderal (early coloniser). Country children of my generation learned to identify and crush dock for the sap that soothes nettle stings – perhaps the most widely used of all folk remedies.
/environment/2026/oct/09/plant-selfie-ja.trail: Stanhope, Weardale: I’ve realised in that time that beauty and fascination can lie in the most mundane of plants – in this case, broad-leaved dock

/environment/2026/oct/09/plant-selfie-ja.headline: Country diary: A little garden mystery – why are the wood mice hoarding opium seeds?
/environment/2026/oct/09/plant-selfie-ja.excerpt: The opium poppies have now set seed, their leaves rattling like crisp packets, the vents beneath their pod lids open for the seeds to be scattered. Dotted throughout my flower borders, adding stature to the vegetable garden, Papaver somniferum is the breadseed poppy, its large, floppy petals unpredictable in colour: pale lilac, purple, pink or sometimes with fringed petals. The unexpected brings a freedom and a randomness to the garden. Those blue-grey seeds are sprinkled on bagels and bread, baked into cakes or ground as a thickener for curries, adding protein, plant fats and trace elements such as manganese. But in its unripe state this is the plant that gives opium, a two-sided drug, both medicinal and destructive as a sedative – its specific name somniferum means sleep-bringing. It is when the petals fall off, leaving a plump, unripe capsule the colour of celadon, that the opium is extracted. Damage the pod or break off a poppy stem, and a white, milky latex oozes out. It is this that contains a mixture of opiate alkaloids including morphine, heroin and codeine, something wildlife would normally avoid. These poppies are also the source of a mystery in my garden. I’m sitting on the terrace in the late afternoon sun, feeling the absence of the swallows, when a wood mouse scampers past. It runs lightly up the stalk of a poppy, one that I’ve been enjoying for its late flowering.
/environment/2026/oct/09/plant-selfie-ja.trail: Allendale, Northumberland: My late-flowering poppies have lit up the garden, and it’s not only me who’s taken an interest

/environment/2026/oct/09/plant-selfie-ja.headline: Trump rollback of US forest protections could accelerate extinction of 400 endangered species
/environment/2026/oct/09/plant-selfie-ja.excerpt: More than 400 endangered animal and plant species could face accelerated extinction after the Donald Trump administration’s decision to rescind a rule that has protected old-growth forests for more than two decades. According to a new report from the Center for Biological Diversity, the rollback of the Bill Clinton-era “roadless rule” could put 7.4m acres (3m hectares) of endangered-species habitat and nearly 1,800 miles (2,900km) of protected rivers and streams at risk, while opening more than 45m acres of national forests to roads, drilling and logging. The Trump administration moved last week to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, citing “outdated restrictions [that] have kept tens of millions of forested acres off-limits to the very treatments that improve forest health and reduce wildfire risk to our communities”. Conservationists have criticized the decision. “Our national forests are home to some of America’s most iconic animals, from grizzlies to hellbenders. These forests provide clean drinking water to countless communities. Bulldozing more roads through them will mean dirtier water, fragmented wildlife habitat and greater wildfire risk,” said Randi Spivak, public lands policy director at the Center for Biological Diversity.

/environment/2026/oct/09/plant-selfie-ja.headline: Country diary: From the beech trees of home to the hot Surrey Hills
/environment/2026/oct/09/plant-selfie-ja.excerpt: At the start of the second heatwave, we visit Jack’s twin and her family in Surrey. From our landmark clump of beech loaded with mast, the car brushes through lanes of rampant deciduous growth woven with bedstraw, honeysuckle and incipient fruits of bramble. Our neighbour’s cut and cleared hayfield overlooks luminous flowers of sweet chestnut, with dead ash in Nanie Rowe’s wood. Across the Tamar, through a patchwork of woods and pastures, we meet the first lorry-load of straw – essential supplies from upcountry needed for winter bedding. By Exeter, the dampness eases off and the motorway cutting through red sandstone reminds me of fertile arable land, much of it encroached on by suburbs. Along slower stretches, I look sideways beyond the ubiquitous ragwort to pick out features such as the wooded eminence of Cadbury Castle. Near Ilchester, Somerset, trailers of chopped “cut-whole” straw stems and unripened grain are carted along the three-lane highway. Ancient lynchets by Mere, Wiltshire, mark the start of proper chalk country, where coombs and winterbournes of rough pasture are interspersed with rolling downland of gold and brown cereals, some already harvested. Leafy green maize will be ensiled for winter fodder. Swags of old man’s beard clothe the bushy verges, and tumuli precede the always spectacular ring of people encircling Stonehenge. Ever closer to London, this nervous passenger shuts her eyes to blot out the lanes filled with lorries and fast-moving traffic.
/environment/2026/oct/09/plant-selfie-ja.trail: St Dominic, Cornwall, to Reigate: Along the way, this nervous passenger passes rolling downlands of cereals, Stonehenge, and of course, lorries loaded up with straw
